doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Being white: growing up in Aliquippa
summary: Asked whether being white affects gigs, he recounts growing up near Plan Eleven and a Catholic high school friendships.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You are a middle-aged white guy. That’s my astute observation. Does that affect getting gigs?

You know, okay, that’s a great question. I’ll go back to when I grew up. I grew up near Pittsburgh in a place called Aliquippa, West Aliquippa, Pennsylvania. And my grandmother, my mother’s mother, lived in a part of Aliquippa which was called Plan Eleven. Now Plan Eleven was all black except one white family, hers. Okay? And when I was a kid we would go there on Sunday to see my grandparents and hang out in the yard and next to the yard was another ball field, where the cats would play, the neighborhood would play. And eventually I would go start playing with them. So I learned how to play sports, you know, with pretty good players. And then I went to high school and I ended up knowing these guys in high school, so I kind of knew them before I got to high school. I went to a Catholic high school in West Aliquippa, which, there was no black people in West Aliquippa. So I never even thought about it, because these guys were my friends, and we used to use racial slurs all the time and it was not, it was nothing, it was like, “Hey man,” “hi dude,” “how you doin’,” and that’s not the words we’d use but that’s the way we talked and it had no problem until I got to New York and I heard I wasn’t supposed to be talking like that. And I said you’ve got to be kidding me. Okay. Now I’m
on the jazz scene where there’s supposed to be racial stuff. And I’ll tell you another story. You ever heard of Stanley Crouch?
